alignment.note: Greek reads ὃς ἂν τόπος ('whatever place'), explicitly naming τόπος as the subject of non-reception; the Vulgate quicumque ('whosoever') and Syriac ܡܢ ('whoever') both render a personal relative rather than a locative, shifting the referent from the place to its inhabitants.

Greek μὴ δέξηται ὑμᾶς, Syriac ܕܠܐ ܢܩܒܠܘܢܟܘܢ, and Vulgate non receperint vos all express the negated reception of 'you' with the object pronoun incorporated; Syriac compresses pronoun into the verbal suffix.

The 'nor hear you' clause is attested by all three: Greek μηδὲ ἀκούσωσιν ὑμῶν, Syriac ܘܠܐ ܢܫܡܥܘܢܟܘܢ, Latin nec audierint vos; again Syriac uses a pronominal verbal suffix where Greek and Latin use a separate genitive/accusative pronoun.

Greek uses a present participle ἐκπορευόμενοι ἐκεῖθεν ('departing thence') and the Vulgate mirrors it with exeuntes inde; the Peshitta expands the construction into a finite temporal clause ܡܐ ܕܢܦܩܝܢ ܐܢܬܘܢ ܡܢ ܬܡܢ ('when you go out from there'), a typical Syriac periphrasis for the Greek circumstantial participle.

Greek employs an articular attributive phrase τὸν ὑποκάτω ('the [dust] which is beneath'); the Vulgate reduces this to the simple preposition de ('from'), while Syriac ܕܒܬܚܬܝܐ retains the relative-prepositional sense ('which is under'), preserving the Greek articular construction more closely than the Latin.

Greek τῶν ποδῶν ὑμῶν and Latin pedibus vestris both express 'your feet' with article/possessive; Syriac ܕܪܓܠܝܟܘܢ collapses the phrase into a single word with a pronominal suffix, an idiomatic compression.

Greek αὐτοῖς ('against/to them', plural) and Latin illis agree; the Peshitta incorporates the testimony-and-pronoun into the single suffixed noun ܠܣܗܕܘܬܗܘܢ ('for their testimony'), so the dative pronoun is realised as a possessive suffix rather than a separate token.

Greek Ἀμὴν and Syriac ܘܐܡܝܢ both transmit the solemn introductory 'Amen, I say to you' formula; the Clementine Vulgate omits the entire 'Amen dico vobis... in die judicii' saying here (Mark 6:11b), reflecting the shorter Western/Vulgate text that lacks the Sodom-and-Gomorrah comparison found in the Byzantine tradition and the Peshitta.

Greek λέγω ὑμῖν encodes the first-person subject within the verb; Syriac analytically supplies the independent pronoun ܐܢܐ ('I') alongside ܐܡܪ and the dative ܠܟܘܢ, a normal Syriac articulation of the Greek synthetic verb.

Greek uses the comparative adjective ἀνεκτότερον ἔσται ('it will be more tolerable'); Syriac renders this with ܕܢܗܘܐ ܢܝܚ ('that it shall be at ease/restful'), employing the noun-like ܢܝܚ (root n-y-kh, 'rest, relief') rather than a morphological comparative, a lexical-construction shift typical of Syriac comparison.

Greek ἢ Γομόρροις ('or for Gomorrah') is matched by Syriac ܘܠܥܡܘܪܐ ('and for Gomorrah'); the Syriac conjunction ܘ ('and') replaces the Greek disjunctive ἤ, treating the two cities as a paired unit rather than alternatives.

Greek ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως ('in the day of judgment') corresponds to Syriac ܒܝܘܡܐ ܕܕܝܢܐ; the Syriac uses the construct/relative ܕ to express the genitive 'of judgment' where Greek uses the bare genitive κρίσεως.

Greek τῇ πόλει ἐκείνῃ ('for that city') is rendered by Syriac ܠܡܕܝܢܬܐ ܗܝ; the Syriac demonstrative ܗܝ follows the noun and the dative is marked by the proclitic ܠ, matching the Greek dative of comparison.
